articles.title: The US Is Losing to China in the Battle of Global Influence
articles.full_text:
China is building a dense network of relationships across all pillars of influence while the United States continues to weaken the institutions it traditionally used to compete.
Heads of state and government participating in the 2024 FOCAC Summit pose for a group photo in Beijing, China, Sep. 5, 2024.
Global influence is frequently a topic for conference panels, talk show pundits, and earnest think tank recommendations, but this nebulous measure of soft power has real-world impact for national security, economic strength and political power.  
Today, this battle is unfolding rapidly, region by region, country by country, through security and commercial partnerships, emerging regional groupings, newly established diplomatic outposts, and academic partnerships.  
As conflicts erupt and new trade and political alignments emerge, it’s clear: China is building a dense network of relationships across all pillars of influence while the United States continues to weaken the institutions it traditionally used to compete. The United States should do more than watch China’s intensive investment in building global influence – in diplomacy, in academic and cultural exchanges, in economic partnerships, and in national security pacts. 
Influence is hard to gauge – and even harder to count on. Even the closest of diplomatic partners have sovereign interests and political differences. Historical relationships, either through war-hardened alliances or postcolonial reckonings, can shape perception and sway alignment. However, China’s transactional approach inherently reflects its genuine disregard for human rights, democratic aspirations, and welfare of citizens in other countries. This is China’s weak point, which the United States can leverage to regain lost ground.  
The work of diplomacy is accomplished behind the scenes, by building connections, negotiating agreements, and advocating for businesses. The work of a diplomat is to know the government officials and trade contacts before you make an ask. This allows diplomats to build the trust required to get to agreement before a crisis happens or an ask is made.  
China is succeeding at one of the first rules of diplomacy: showing up. 
The Lowry Institute’s Global Diplomacy Index paints a clear picture. China has 274 diplomatic posts globally, compared with the United States’ 271. The strategic advantage is even clearer in Africa – where China has 60 to the United States’ 56 – and in East Asia, where China has 44 to the United States’ 27.  While the numerical difference is small, the trend is concerning. 
Beijing leverages its growing diplomatic presence as a strategic asset, populating its embassies with commercial, educational, and political professionals. It is gradually making inroads even with the United States’ longtime partners. Just this month, China’s President Xi Jinping traveled to Egypt, where Beijing and Cairo signed an array of agreements, from linking Egypt’s national development plan to China’s Belt and Road Initiative to a pledge to increase trade and investments in their own currencies, moving away from the U.S. dollar. 
For the United States, the trend is going the other way, and that’s worrying. Despite a slate of recent nominations, 93 out of 196 ambassadorial slots remain vacant, according to the tracker maintained by the American Foreign Service Association. And while in many cases there are able professional diplomats serving as chargés d’affaires in these roles, a confirmed ambassador signals seriousness to host governments.  
The State Department has also taken steps to close a number of smaller consulates and shrink operations at other embassies. While there is absolutely a strong case for prioritizing engagement, streamlining operations, and improving efficiencies, the narrative that the United States is retreating from the world continues to spread. 
Academic opportunities and cultural exchanges are important forms of diplomacy and a path to increasing the United States’ global influence. Engaging with the next generations of global talent is a critical investment or opportunity, and China understands this.  
At the 2024 Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC), Xi announced 60,000 government scholarships for African students. In addition to opportunities for students, FOCAC commitments will see some 20,000 African regional and city leaders receiving training in China every year, along with African journalists sent to China.  
These programs are far from boondoggles: They enmesh these emerging officials, journalists, and business leaders into Chinese institutions and professional networks. And despite warnings from the United States, China has now established over 500 Confucius Institutes around the world. These institutes are purported to facilitate Chinese education and people-to-people exchanges, but effectively serve as propaganda arms of the Chinese government.  
The United States has extraordinary assets of its own, including an open and free democracy, the best universities in the world, and an innovation economy. Traditionally, U.S. government-supported exchange programs showcase all three.  
From the International Visitor Leadership Program (IVLP), which identifies rising stars in business, government, security, and media and brings them to the United States to showcase America’s story to world-class State Department programs, including the Fulbright, Gilman, Boren, and Critical Language Scholarships, these programs engage professionals at key junctures in their professional careers.  
A scholarship or an exchange isn’t simply tuition assistance. These academic and cultural programs create alumni who may become government and business leaders in their countries. According to the State Department’s own accounting, over 500 IVLP alumni alone have become heads of state or government since the program’s founding in 1940. Another 12 have won Nobel Prizes, and thousands more have served as elected officials, government ministers, and community and business leaders. 
The United States can benefit from having these leaders as counterparts; they leave these programs with firsthand knowledge and appreciation of America’s economic strength, tech savvy, entrepreneurship, pluralism, and values. 
These programs continue, albeit after some stutters in funding in 2025. Yet there are deep proposed reductions in the 2027 fiscal year’s budget. And there is a long-term cost to making such programs unpredictable. China is rapidly expanding its networks, while the United States is offering uncertainty into its own powerful equivalents.  
Economic Strength: Building Partnerships, Not Transactions 
This isn’t a new trend. Pundits have warned for more than two decades that Beijing is approaching traditional U.S. partners with something tangible to offer.  
Through its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), as well as smaller bilateral and regional deals, China has smartly offered financing backed by its government for desperately needed infrastructure projects linked to access to African and Western Hemisphere markets.  
At the most recent FOCAC summit in 2024, Xi announced approximately $51 billion in financial support to Africa over a three-year period. At the 2025 China-Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC) Forum, Xi pledged a credit line of more than $9 billion for Latin America, as well as additional bilateral infrastructure investment. According to China’s own accounting in its 2025 BRI Investment Report, agreements that are part of BRI reached over $213 billion in 2025, up 75 percent from the previous year, with about 150 countries participating. 
The United States can compete. The Lobito Corridor, which links Zambia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Angola, provides U.S. support for a critical rail and infrastructure network spanning mineral production to port facilities. Through a $533 million loan from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), the United States both invested in these countries’ economic development and leveraged this financing with an eye to long-term regional security through employment, investment, and regional integration.  
However, while the United States has (and uses) smart tools like the DFC and Millenium Challenge Corporation, it has stopped some other initiatives. Driven by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), the 2025 reprioritization of foreign assistance sidelined early-stage economic development efforts, such as programs for emerging entrepreneurs, small business, and agriculture – including dedicated programs to encourage women in these fields. These and other opportunities were once administered through the now-shuttered USAID and State Department programs. The 2025 foreign assistance restructuring halted these incubator projects worldwide, ending a values-based and long-term approach to economic growth. 
While reform of U.S. assistance was absolutely necessary, the geopolitical cost is clear. When the United States – with its commitment to human rights, democracy, rule of law, and anti-corruption measures – withdraws from a relationship, it is often China that surges to occupy the space. 
Today, faced with the immediate challenge of global leadership in artificial intelligence (AI), the United States must be more than the leader in a technology footrace with China. The U.S. global role and responsibilities will require sustained investment in innovation, talent, infrastructure and trusted partnerships so the United States can continue in setting global standards that shape how AI is developed, governed and deployed. The United States can build on its standards of openness and accountability while ensuring that these emerging technologies reflect both U.S. interests and U.S. values. 
China is intensifying its investment in its initiatives, building a worldwide network of infrastructure, finance, commercial, and political relationships. The United States absolutely has best-in-class competitive alternatives, but Washington must invest in and deepen those ties.  
Many countries, especially across the Global South, see benefits to relationships with both China and the United States, but U.S. strength has traditionally meant that it is the first choice for security relationships, cultural and educational exchanges, and business partnerships. China’s approach has significant and public weaknesses, including debt controversies, debates over its political influence, and allegations of exploitation and human rights abuses in partner countries.
articles.summary: China is building a dense network of relationships across all pillars of influence while the United States continues to weaken the institutions it traditionally used to compete.

articles.title: Philippine Energy Security Could Determine the Outcome of a Taiwan Contingency
articles.full_text:
Any Sino-American conflict would place enormous pressure on fuel supplies. U.S. fuel dependence turns Manila’s energy fragility into a strategic vulnerability.
A U.S. Marine assigned to I Marine Expeditionary Force transports a fuel hose during a specialized fueling operation in support of Exercise Balikatan 2026 at Cagayan North International Airport, Lal-lo, Philippines, Apr. 25, 2026.
In March, a U.S. ally declared a “state of energy emergency” after experiencing disruptions to its crude deliveries. After gaining a waiver from Washington, Petron, the Philippines’ only refinery, bought Russian oil. The episode exposed a decades-old vulnerability in U.S. strategy: Philippine fuel insecurity.
Beginning in 2010, across three Pacific tours, I’ve watched China erode regional security through its increased power and aggression. For the United States to deter China from a Taiwan annexation attempt, it requires access to the Philippines and its oil. However, a conflict that draws in the U.S. will likely disrupt the Philippine oil imports that sustain American operations.
The Philippines sits at the Pacific’s crossroads, in the middle of the First Island Chain, connecting Taiwan and the South China Sea. The Philippines’ placement makes it vital to U.S. deterrence. Economically, this region carries 43 percent of global crude shipments and 21 percent of trade. Geographically, control of the Luzon Strait would allow China to isolate Taiwan.
For 20 years, Chinese coercion has revealed Beijing’s desire to control these crossroads, annex Taiwan, and dominate the Pacific. To deter China and sustain American operations 6,500 miles from California, the U.S. needs reliable access to the Philippines and its oil. Yet Manila’s small, nearly import-only oil industry leaves it and U.S. forces vulnerable.
During my last tour in the Pacific, then-Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan. China’s response, and its subsequent isolation “rehearsals,” demonstrated its power and aggression. Several isolation zones extended across the Luzon Strait, and, based on recent events, Beijing intends to contest Philippine sovereignty in these areas.
Luzon is critical to deterring “a conflict over Taiwan” and safeguarding global shipping routes, because it’s within ground-based missile range of Taiwan. For China to annex Taiwan, it must control the Luzon Strait to blockade Taiwan, threaten Philippine sovereignty, and degrade U.S. intervention. However, if the United States can maintain reliable access, it can resupply Taiwan and deny a Chinese annexation operation.
But geography is only one part of the equation. Operations from Luzon depend on reliable Philippine oil. American fuel dependence turns Manila’s energy fragility into a strategic vulnerability.
In 2022, the U.S. Department of Defense required over 73 million barrels for operations, training, and exercises globally, with 48 percent purchased overseas. Unsurprisingly, air and maritime operations account for 91 percent of demand, roughly 66.5 million barrels. Any Sino-American conflict would place enormous pressure on fuel supplies thousands of miles from the U.S. homeland.
The Philippines alone consumes 474,000 barrels per day and maintains only a 40-45 day reserve. Since Caltex and Shell closed their refineries, Petron has capacity to support only a limited share of national demand. Manila relies on imports, with almost 97 percent of crude coming from the Middle East and nearly 95 percent of refined products coming from Asia.
In a crisis, U.S. demands on Philippine oil would rapidly deplete Manila’s reserves. At the same time, Chinese maritime interdiction operations in the South China Sea would disrupt Philippine import routes and constrain American operations. The result would be another “state of energy emergency.”
Proven Philippine oil reserves stand at 139 million barrels, with another 202 million more locked in Bangsamoro’s Liguasan Marsh, which is a historical insurgency hotspot. Developing these resources and expanding refining capacity strengthens Manila’s resiliency. It’s also a mutually beneficial opportunity for Philippine-U.S. commercial cooperation.
Currently, the Pentagon is building extra oil capacity in Davao to “enable U.S. naval vessels to receive fuel.” The new depot is a positive step forward, but its limited capacity and continuous resupply needs mean that storage alone cannot solve the underlying problem.
American security requires more than stockpiles; it requires stronger Philippine extraction and refining capacity. The U.S.-Venezuela framework offers one possible model. This year, several U.S.-based oil companies signed agreements to develop Venezuelan reserves in support of both countries’ interests. The Philippine context differs, but the underlying mechanism, a bilateral agreement to unlock private-sector investment in domestic production, could be adapted to Washington’s and Manila’s needs.
Many existing Philippine-U.S. energy programs cover renewables, nuclear power, energy costs, and critical minerals, but none specifically targets Manila’s weak fuel extraction, refining, and distribution system. The November ASEAN Summit in Manila, where U.S. President Donald Trump and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. may meet, offers an opportunity.
Washington should create a targeted Philippine oil resilience program directly linked to U.S. strategy. An ideal model to emulate is the Philippines Energy Threshold Program. Both nations’ commercial investment sectors can strengthen Manila’s fuel security and expand its capacity. To be sure, one program cannot address every wartime need, but it will reduce U.S. vulnerabilities.
My proposal benefits both nations’ prosperity, commercial industries, and U.S. strategy. From my tours, I’ve seen how oil underpins strategy. In a Sino-American conflict, we cannot assume fuel will arrive. Both nations should create an oil resilience program now, before the crisis begins.

articles.title: How to Fix South Korea-Ukraine Relations
articles.full_text:
Clear ground rules could not only help resolve the North Korean POW standoff but prevent the next case.
The transfer of two North Korean soldiers to South Korea was intended to be a quiet diplomatic success. Ukraine captured them in January 2025 while they were fighting for Russia in the Kursk region. After months of bilateral talks, they arrived in South Korea in mid-September. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the transfer at the U.N. General Assembly on September 23. That started a spat that culminated in South Korea recalling its ambassador to Ukraine on October 8, its first protest recall since 2008. 
Seoul is still demanding acknowledgment and an apology, while Kyiv considers the matter closed. On October 20, Seoul announced plans to withdraw roughly half its embassy personnel, citing what it described as Ukraine’s failure to take constructive steps to resolve the dispute.
Ukraine had a clear strategic interest in drawing the world’s attention to North Korea’s participation in Russia’s war. Instead, the episode exposed something else: a lack of sufficiently clear ground rules for managing the sensitive political consequences of South Korea-Ukraine cooperation.
Nearly a month after Zelenskyy’s revelation, the two governments still can’t agree on what they agreed on in terms of confidentiality. Seoul says confidentiality governed the talks from the start, even though no formal nondisclosure document was signed. It says internal records support that account and that it told Kyiv before Zelenskyy’s speech not to breach the understanding. Kyiv initially denied that a confidentiality agreement existed; Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha later said the dispute stemmed from differing interpretations of the confidentiality requirements at various stages of the transfer.
Sybiha’s explanation points to the more useful lesson. An informal diplomatic understanding is not inherently defective, but whatever understandings and consultation process existed were not enough to prevent the disclosure dispute. Seoul had substantial reasons for discretion, including possible risks to the soldiers and their relatives who remain in North Korea. Ukraine had strong motives for publicity: North Korean troops are participating in the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, and more are expected to arrive on the frontlines. 
South Korea’s intelligence service has also told lawmakers that Ukraine originally requested secrecy, partly because the transfer of North Korean POWs could invite criticism that Ukraine had forgone a possible prisoner-exchange opportunity. If that account is correct, the incentives for secrecy and publicity shifted over time. Agreements that must survive shifting incentives need to be written down.
Of course, given the lack of clarity around confidentiality, Kyiv should have consulted with Seoul rather than proceeding with a public announcement. South Korea was justified in demanding an explanation and safeguards to prevent a recurrence. Ukraine later sent language that South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said contained an apology, but Seoul deemed it insufficient. Kyiv later declared the controversy closed. 
For now, the two governments are stuck defending incompatible accounts of the past. What they should be doing is figuring out how to handle the next case.
The deeper problem is that the issues passing through their bilateral channels have evolved faster than the practices for handling them. To give an idea of the robustness – or lack thereof – of bilateral mechanisms before Russia’s invasion, the eighth round of foreign ministry political consultations in 2019 came after a seven-year gap and focused largely on conventional bilateral diplomacy. 
As recently as September 16, a week before Zelenskyy’s speech, Ukrainian officials were discussing reviving those consultations. But the older platforms for discussion aren’t fit for purpose anymore. After North Korean troops entered Russia’s war, Zelenskyy and then-South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol agreed in October 2024 to intensify intelligence and expertise exchanges. Their foreign ministers have discussed battlefield conditions, North Korean prisoners, and Russia-North Korea military cooperation. In 2019, they were talking about “trade, investment, science, technology, and agriculture” – far less sensitive topics.
That means the same questions are likely to recur in South Korea-Ukraine relations. Ukrainian forces encounter North Korean troops and weapons in combat; South Korea wants to know what those encounters reveal about tactics, missile performance, battlefield adaptation, and Russian assistance. Future cases could involve another prisoner, captured equipment, debriefing materials, sanctions intelligence, or evidence of Russian technology transfers. Each could raise the same basic questions: what information is jointly sensitive, who may disclose it, and what happens if the other government objects?
Ukraine’s foreign minister has called the two countries “natural allies,” but Seoul has not adopted Kyiv’s strategic position toward Russia and continues to withhold direct lethal assistance. Seoul has its own reasons to preserve diplomatic space with Moscow and Pyongyang. The two governments do not need identical interests, but they do need ground rules for handling the information they are already sharing. 
First, South Korea and Ukraine should define confidentiality in writing. For jointly handled information or information shared under agreed restrictions, the two governments should document what is protected, how long the restriction applies, and who may authorize disclosure. In the POW spat, Kyiv’s first response was to deny that any agreement existed; a written text would have clearly established the existence and scope of any commitment.
Second, an objection should trigger a defined escalation process. Advance notice was insufficient in the POW case. Kyiv warned that Zelenskyy would speak at the U.N. and might raise the case, and Seoul responded by objecting to public disclosure. But the speech went ahead, even though the disagreement remained unresolved. Future cases should require another round of consultation when either government objects to disclosure – first among the officials handling the issue and, if necessary, between senior political offices. That would not guarantee compromise, nor should it give either government an indefinite veto over the other’s public statements. It would move the disagreement to a point where compromise remains possible.
Third, South Korea and Ukraine need to give Russia-North Korea security cooperation a standing, quiet place within the bilateral relationship. If Seoul and Kyiv do revive their political consultations, those talks should include a regular security track to compare assessments of North Korean battlefield performance, weapons, Russian assistance, North Korean personnel returning from the war, and other lessons relevant to the Korean Peninsula. Their existing intelligence and expertise exchanges should feed into this track. 
The point is continuity: officials should not have to rebuild priorities, contacts, and disclosure boundaries every time a new incident forces the issue. The same track should host the written terms and escalation contacts, so officials who know one another can try to resolve an objection before it reaches the leaders.
These principles could help resolve the current standoff. Seoul wants Ukraine to acknowledge that confidentiality was part of the talks; Kyiv maintains that there was never a firm agreement. A possible compromise would acknowledge that confidentiality was discussed, that the two sides understood its scope differently, and that future sensitive cases will use written terms and a defined consultation process before any disclosure. The first two elements broadly align with Sybiha’s own formula, so the statement would ask Kyiv to concede less than it may seem. 
Ukraine could also express regret for any added risk to soldiers’ relatives. That would differ from the regret Kyiv’s Foreign Ministry has expressed so far, which focused on the dispute’s escalation into public criticism, and would give Seoul something closer to the acknowledgment it has sought. Such a statement would not require Seoul to abandon its account of the negotiations or Kyiv to admit a deliberate breach. Three European governments have reportedly offered to help ease tensions, suggesting that outside assistance may be available.
Even as Seoul reduces its diplomatic presence in Kyiv, it says humanitarian and reconstruction support for Ukraine will continue. Still, the expanding confrontation shows how difficult it can be to keep one grievance from overshadowing broader cooperation. Ground rules will not eliminate the larger differences between the two governments – Seoul’s interest in preserving room for dialogue with Pyongyang and Kyiv’s in exposing North Korea’s role in the war – and leaders can always ignore procedures. But a written agreement and clear procedures for handling disclosure will help head off similar cases before they erupt into public view.
Russia and North Korea have built a partnership suited to the war they are now fighting together. Seoul and Kyiv don’t need a formal alliance, but they do need better channels to handle the sensitive information that’s now a part of their partnership: the next prisoner, the next captured weapon, the next intelligence finding, and the next disagreement over who gets to tell the world.

articles.title: Censorship in Pakistan Goes From ‘Pleasant’ to ‘Unpleasant’
articles.full_text:
Authorities have directed satellite TV channels to refrain from broadcasting or providing live coverage of “unpleasant incidents,” meaning shootings, blasts and terrorist attacks.
The famous Pakistani satirist and playwright, Anwar Maqsood, once said at the Karachi Literature Festival: “The biggest lie in Pakistan is PTV’s weather report. Outside it is scorching hot, but the news announces: ‘The weather across the country is pleasant.'”
The man, a master of puns and wordplay, used the weather analogy to highlight the censorship imposed on the state broadcaster to keep people away from the harsh realities of the country. He used “scorching hot” as a metaphor for unemployment, inflation, poverty and social unrest.
Now, things have gone from “pleasant” to “unpleasant.”
The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) on October 13 directed satellite television channels to refrain from broadcasting or providing live coverage of “unpleasant incidents,” meaning explosions, blasts, firing and terrorist attacks.
“All satellite TV channel licensees are once again hereby directed to refrain from broadcast, re-broadcast and live coverage of any unfortunate/unpleasant incident such as explosion, blast, firing, terrorist attack etc,” the notification said, adding, “Satellite TV channels must broadcast only such verified information, warranted by the concerned department/law enforcement agency.”
The notification also directed channels to “effectively use time delay mechanism” and ensure the constitution of an independent editorial board in accordance with PEMRA laws, a Supreme Court judgment in suo motu case No. 28 of 2018, and an Islamabad High Court order issued on September 5, 2022.
Before the PEMRA notification, Pakistani satellite TV channels had refrained from broadcasting the “most unpleasant” – the name of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan and his image. Following the May 9, 2023, protests triggered by Khan’s arrest, PEMRA asked television licensees to ensure that “hate mongers, rioters, their facilitators and perpetrators” were “completely screened out from media.” Although it did not name Khan, television channels got the message.
Now, TV anchors have devised a new nomenclature while referring to news regarding Khan’s court proceedings. The preferred terms are “chairman Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)” or “PTI chief.” One TV anchor satirically uses “Kasim ke Abba” (father of Kasim), which is the name of Khan’s elder son.
Recently, Pakistani journalist and author Mohammed Hanif, in his satirical blog on BBC Urdu, said people of his age had seen posters saying, “Please avoid political discussions in Pakistani restaurants.” Hanif says that, though he has not seen any restaurant owner pushing guests out for indulging in political discussion, this rule will now be implemented by Pakistan’s cyber authorities.
Any comment or discussion can be construed as anti-national or as disturbing public peace because the cyber authorities have not specified what constitutes such content. So, even a harmless post can invite the government’s wrath if a comment below it is seen as an attack on a government department. In the end, Hanif suggests that the safest way to avoid the midnight knock on your door is to discuss cooking recipes.

Now, TV anchors have devised a new nomenclature while referring to news regarding Khan’s court proceedings. The preferred terms are “chairman Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)” or “PTI chief.” One TV anchor satirically uses “Kasim ke Abba” (father of Kasim), which is the name of Khan’s elder son.
Recently, Pakistani journalist and author Mohammed Hanif, in his satirical blog on BBC Urdu, said people of his age had seen posters saying, “Please avoid political discussions in Pakistani restaurants.” Hanif says that, though he has not seen any restaurant owner pushing guests out for indulging in political discussion, this rule will now be implemented by Pakistan’s cyber authorities.
Any comment or discussion can be construed as anti-national or as disturbing public peace because the cyber authorities have not specified what constitutes such content. So, even a harmless post can invite the government’s wrath if a comment below it is seen as an attack on a government department. In the end, Hanif suggests that the safest way to avoid the midnight knock on your door is to discuss cooking recipes.
The famous Pakistani satirist and playwright, Anwar Maqsood, once said at the Karachi Literature Festival: “The biggest lie in Pakistan is PTV’s weather report. Outside it is scorching hot, but the news announces: ‘The weather across the country is pleasant.'”
The man, a master of puns and wordplay, used the weather analogy to highlight the censorship imposed on the state broadcaster to keep people away from the harsh realities of the country. He used “scorching hot” as a metaphor for unemployment, inflation, poverty and social unrest.
Asif Ullah Khan is a veteran journalist who has held senior editorial positions at The Times of India, Khaleej Times, The Hindustan Times, and The Brunei Times. He currently writes for The Diplomat, The Wire, The India Legal, The ASEAN Post, and other international publications.
articles.summary: Authorities have directed satellite TV channels to refrain from broadcasting or providing live coverage of "unpleasant incidents," meaning shootings, blasts and terrorist attacks.

articles.title: Hong Kong’s Vanishing Rainbow Shows How China’s Social Control Travels
articles.full_text:
From Hong Kong to Bangkok, Paris, Taiwan, and North America, LGBTQ communities are encountering censorship, surveillance, and coercive pressure linked to China.
The Hong Kong Pride Parade in 2014. The full event hasn’t been held since 2018.
China’s growing pressure on LGBTQ communities is increasingly transnational. Chinese nationals who attend Pride events overseas can attract police attention after returning home; overseas Chinese LGBTQ groups remain vulnerable to censorship on Chinese platforms; cultural spaces in Europe can lose access to Chinese social media for promoting transgender films; and mainland writers publishing gay fiction on overseas platforms have faced prosecution at home. Hong Kong offers a particularly revealing entry point because similar pressures are visible there even though same-sex relationships are legal (though not legally recognized as marriages).
In October, the organizing committee of Hong Kong Pride canceled its annual Rainbow Market at Central Market after being told that an administrative error had resulted in double-booking. Organizers had already received confirmation, paid a deposit, and announced the venue.
The cancellation followed a wider pattern. Earlier in 2026, Pink Dot HK, the city’s largest annual LGBTQ carnival, canceled its event after the operator of Stanley Plaza and Murray House withdrew the venues, citing unresolved licensing issues. It was the second consecutive year in which Pink Dot failed to proceed. In 2025, negotiations to hold the event at West Kowloon Cultural District’s Art Park had also collapsed. 
Hong Kong Pride itself lost a planned venue at Kwun Tong Promenade in 2025 after organizers had already paid rent and announced the event.
These cases illustrate how LGBTQ public life in Hong Kong is being narrowed through administrative and institutional means rather than formal criminal prohibition. Consensual same-sex conduct remains legal, and LGBTQ organizations continue to exist. But these groups find it harder and harder to organize publicly, retain venues, sustain institutions, and remain visible in civic life.
This is striking because Hong Kong once had one of the most visible LGBTQ communities in East Asia. The city decriminalized consensual homosexual conduct between adult men in 1991, while its courts later expanded legal protections for same-sex couples in areas including immigration, taxation, and public housing. Social acceptance also rose significantly. Survey research published in 2023 found that 69 percent of respondents were “moderately” or “very accepting” of gay men and lesbians, while 60 percent supported same-sex marriage and 71 percent supported anti-discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation.
Hong Kong Pride once drew thousands into the streets, but its last full Pride march took place in 2018. In 2019, police declined permission for a march amid the citywide protests and permitted only a static rally. Pandemic restrictions later pushed Pride activities online, after which organizers shifted toward indoor markets and smaller events. The large public march never returned.
Most LGBTQ organizations in Hong Kong were never primarily political in the conventional sense. Their work focused on discrimination, health, family acceptance, culture, community support, and legal equality. Their shrinking space therefore shows how Hong Kong’s post-2020 transformation has moved beyond suppressing explicit political opposition and into regulating autonomous social life.
The same pattern is visible in mainland China. China decriminalized homosexuality in 1997 and removed homosexuality from its official classification of mental disorders in 2001 (in practice, if not in actual fact). During the 2000s and early 2010s, LGBTQ organizations, university groups, online communities, and cultural events expanded in major cities. Under Xi Jinping, that space has contracted sharply. Shanghai Pride ceased operations in 2020, the Beijing LGBT Center closed in 2023, university LGBTQ groups have faced mounting restrictions, and social media accounts associated with sexual minority organizations have been deleted or suspended.
Foreign connections have become increasingly important to this repression. Chinese authorities often treat independent organizations with international ties as possible channels of foreign influence. LGBTQ groups are especially exposed because contemporary sexual minority advocacy is highly transnational, involving foreign NGOs, embassies, academic institutions, cultural organizations, and legal networks. This allows questions of private identity and social equality to be reframed as questions of sovereignty and political security.
The reach of this logic now extends beyond China’s borders. In 2026, France’s Le Monde reported that Chinese nationals who had participated in Bangkok Pride later received police attention after returning to China. How the authorities identified them remains unclear, but participation in a lawful LGBTQ event in Thailand had become a matter of interest to Chinese police.
This fits within the broader discussion of transnational repression, but LGBTQ communities also reveal a related form of cross-border control that operates through information systems. Chinese platforms and censorship practices increasingly project domestic restrictions into overseas Chinese-speaking communities.
The Chinese Rainbow Network illustrates this problem. The organization operates overseas, yet material on its WeChat public account became inaccessible. Citizen Lab had already shown the structural basis for such control when it found that content exchanged between non-China-registered WeChat accounts could still be subjected to analysis for politically sensitive material. Overseas users can therefore remain inside an information environment shaped by the political requirements of the Chinese party-state.
Recent cases involving the  LGBTQ community show how this extends to cultural expression. The Paris-based Chinese-language cultural space 8lithèque reportedly had its Xiaohongshu (RedNote) account banned after promoting a screening of a transgender-themed film. The event was taking place in France, but the organizers remained vulnerable to the content rules of a Chinese platform.
The Haitang Literature City prosecutions show another dimension of this expanding reach. Haitang, a Taiwan-based platform, became popular among mainland Chinese writers of danmei and boys’ love fiction, including sexually explicit material. Chinese authorities later summoned, detained, and prosecuted mainland writers who had published on the platform, citing China’s obscenity laws. The platform was outside mainland China, but the writers were not beyond the reach of Chinese law enforcement.
Taken together, these cases show how China’s control increasingly travels through people, platforms, and language communities. Whether joining a cultural space in Paris, a platform in Taiwan, a Pride parade in Bangkok, or a community organization in North America, Chinese citizens and Chinese-language communities remain exposed to censorship, surveillance, or coercive pressure originating from inside China.
Why should LGBTQ communities matter so much to the party-state?
One reason is autonomous organization. Community centers, university societies, legal aid groups, online networks, cultural organizations, and Pride events create horizontal ties among citizens outside structures supervised by the Communist Party. Chinese authorities have become increasingly suspicious of such organization across many fields, including labor rights, feminism, religion, public health, and environmental activism.
Sexual minority rights also raise broader questions about pluralism. The principle that individuals should retain dignity and rights even when they depart from majority social norms places limits on the authority of the state, family, and society over private identity.
Family structure adds another dimension. Under Xi Jinping, official discourse has placed growing emphasis on marriage, reproduction, family responsibility, and demographic duty. These themes have become more prominent as China confronts low fertility, population decline, delayed marriage, and rapid aging. Women are increasingly encouraged to marry and have children, while official rhetoric emphasizes “good family traditions” and reproductive responsibility.
LGBTQ identities sit uneasily within this model because they challenge the assumption that adult life should culminate in heterosexual marriage and biological reproduction. They also complicate fixed gender roles within the family.
These tensions acquire greater political significance because Xi has tied social order to the broader project of the “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.” The Communist Party increasingly presents itself as a guardian of Chinese civilizational continuity and social morality.
This emphasis on tradition also represents a shift in the party’s own ideological history. The early People’s Republic was explicitly revolutionary in its approach to family hierarchy. The 1950 Marriage Law attacked arranged marriage, concubinage, male superiority, and other practices described as remnants of the feudal family system. Maoist discourse framed women’s emancipation as part of the destruction of inherited social hierarchy.
Mao-era China was never sexually liberal, but the contrast shows that the Communist Party’s current appeal to traditional family values is selective rather than timeless. During the revolutionary period, dismantling inherited hierarchies served the party’s claim to be creating a new society. Under Xi, family hierarchy, reproductive responsibility, and civilizational continuity serve a different political purpose by reinforcing social order and distinguishing Chinese values from supposedly foreign liberal influence.
LGBTQ communities therefore sit at the intersection of several Xi-era concerns: autonomous organization, minority rights, gender hierarchy, demographic policy, foreign influence, and individual autonomy.
Repression can be effective at weakening the organizational capacity of such groups. Authorities can close community centers, prevent events, delete accounts, restrict fundraising, discourage international partnerships, and make public participation more risky. But these measures cannot remove the identities and experiences that produced these communities.
That creates a long-term political problem. Concepts such as constitutionalism or representative government can remain abstract for citizens who encounter them mainly through rhetoric. Sexuality and gender are experienced through everyday life. Government policy reaches LGBTQ people through relationships, family formation, public expression, employment, access to community, and the ability to describe oneself openly. Feminists encounter a similar dynamic when state-defined expectations concerning marriage, reproduction, and gender roles collide with their own lives.
Repeated discrimination turns political authority into a personal experience. Not every LGBTQ person or feminist will become politically oppositional, but a state that continually restricts people at the level of identity, family, and bodily autonomy risks creating durable alienation that cannot easily be displaced by nationalism or civilizational rhetoric.
articles.summary: From Hong Kong to Bangkok, Paris, Taiwan, and North America, LGBTQ communities are encountering censorship, surveillance, and coercive pressure linked to China.

articles.title: UNDP Asia-Pacific Director Kanni Wignaraja on the Necessity of Redefining Security
articles.full_text:
“If governments are serious about security in the fullest sense, investment in development is non-negotiable.”
In an age of intersectional crises, of threats that bleed across borders and between sectors, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) believes what’s needed is a redefinition of security. In a new report, the UNDP argues that development ought to have a larger role in addressing insecurity – not as it is traditionally understood, but as it actually affects people across Asia and the Pacific. 
It’s not about making a binary choice between defense and development, Kanni Wignaraja, UNDP regional director for Asia and the Pacific, told The Diplomat’s Managing Editor Catherine Putz. Instead, what’s critical is getting the balance right, investing in development and prevention, and leveraging development to enhance security. 
In pursuit of this, the UNDP proposes in its report a framework of “development circuit breakers” addressing economic insecurity, weak institutions, digital disruption and climate-health pressures that interact and reinforce each other. 
“Trust is the one switch that allows all four circuit breakers to work. Each switch depends on trust: between people and institutions, and among the institutions responsible for different parts of the system,” Wignaraja said.
In the following interview, Wignaraja expands on the structural vulnerabilities that define the modern security landscape, puts defense spending trends in context, and urges regional governments to shift their mindset from managing individual crises to managing shared risks.
What structural vulnerabilities define the modern security landscape across Asia and the Pacific? How is the current reality different from previous periods, what’s changed?
A lot has changed in the way we see and feel vulnerability and insecurity today across the region and the world.
Previously, maybe there were more episodic periods of intense pain, wars, for example, but more contained. Now I feel it’s almost like having chronic pain. It’s all of the time and in so many more places. And that is a very different scenario of insecurity and feeling unsafe.
Countries face overlapping shocks, often before they have recovered from the last. The old crisis-recovery-rebuilding cycle is breaking down, putting hard-won development gains repeatedly at risk.
The nature of the threats has changed too: many are not contained within borders. Climate shocks, pandemics, cybercrime, disinformation, supply-chain disruptions and water insecurity move across countries and systems. The scale is enormous. Online criminal economies are estimated at $1.03 trillion annually, with $114.1 billion in losses to cybercrime victims in 2025.
There is also an exponential factor, as these risks now travel faster, connect more quickly and spread like wildfires. Economic insecurity can erode trust; climate shocks destroy livelihoods and strain public finances; weak institutions create space for illicit economies. Sri Lanka illustrates the connections, amid its economic crisis, poverty rose from 11 percent in 2019 to more than 25 percent in 2023, alongside wider social and political unrest. Myanmar shows what can happen when several pressures converge and collide. Conflict, economic decline, poverty, weak governance and criminal economies increasingly reinforce one another. These cannot be neatly separated into security problems on the one hand and development problems on the other.
Our response systems were built for episodic emergencies. They now have to manage chronic, connected insecurity. 
Defense spending is soaring across the world, including in Asia, while development budgets have been trimmed down, in some cases dramatically. Do these trends reflect – or do they ignore – the actual threats communities across Asia and the Pacific face?
Today recorded military budgets are close to US$3 trillion. At the same time official development assistance (ODA) has fallen to $175 billion. This is just 6 cents to the dollar if we compare the ratio between the two. 
We are not arguing to choose between defense and development but getting the balance of investment right. And to optimize security spending that aligns with development outcomes. The questions is how to use both military and development budgets to invest in common outcomes. That’s the win-win. And how do you leverage one to get more of the other?
Military, police and intelligence institutions remain essential. And their budgets can also be a frontline to ensure dual outcomes that ensure national and people’s safety and well-being. 
Investments in technology that enhances wellbeing with protection, early warning and preparedness systems, vaccine production and access, AI integrity and strong rule of law and justice institutions prevent risks from becoming crises. 
Wherever the money comes from, we need to invest much more deliberately in prevention, and for the longer term. Each dollar invested in prevention can mean up to $103 in avoided conflict and crisis costs. For example, in the Philippines anticipatory systems can reach 125,000 vulnerable people three days before a Category 4 or 5 typhoon, before assets and savings are lost. 
Some of the new risks also require us to work differently. Cyber scams are a good example: they combine cybercrime, human trafficking, illicit finance and organized crime, and in many case promote cross border conflict. No single institution can make a dent in this. 
Ultimately, it is about getting a better security return from the investments we make. And where together, one-plus-one can be way beyond two. The opportunity is to find these investments that strengthen both.
What is meant by “the securitization of development” and why is it important to avoid securitizing development as you encourage governments to rethink the connections between development and security?
The risk is that development could come to be seen primarily through a security lens. Development through the lens of human wellbeing must remain an objective in its own right. That is reducing poverty, eliminating major diseases, a full education and decent jobs, affordable energy, water and food for all, protecting rights and enabling people to live with dignity.
The report argues that sustaining security – which is about a safer present and future for all not just a few – cannot be achieved without development defined as improved human wellbeing for all. Investing in people, institutions and resilience is not separate from security but is one of the most effective ways to achieve it. That is different from turning development into a security instrument. Development and security are mutually reinforcing.
Incentives matter. Development should be about enabling people to live free from fear, free from want and in dignity, expanding people’s capabilities, strengthening rights, improving access to services and creating opportunities.
This is why the report places such emphasis on people-centered security. Individuals and communities should be at the heart of both development policy and security decisions. These are not alternative or conflicting choices. Security seen through this lens is about whether people can feel safe in their homes, protect their livelihoods, access justice and basic services, and live without fear. That is very much the human security tradition that UNDP has championed since the early 1990s.
The central message is that if governments are serious about security in the fullest sense, investment in development is non-negotiable. Effective governance, economic opportunity, social protection, digital resilience, climate adaptation and access to justice are not substitutes for security; they are among its most important foundations.
One section of the report states that “Current responses generate the crises they were meant to prevent,” in reference to what’s termed “the response and reactive trap.” Why is it so difficult for regional governments to invest in prevention? How can governments break out of this particular trap?
The fundamental problem with prevention is that when it works, it is often invisible. Political and budget cycles reward visible results, while the return on prevention is often a crisis that did not occur. This makes it easier to finance response and reconstruction than investments that could have reduced the losses in the first place.
We have to make prevention politically meaningful, economically visible and financially viable. That means translating risks into investments with clearer costs, returns and avoided losses. We need to move from paying for disasters to investing in resilience before they happen.
articles.summary: “If governments are serious about security in the fullest sense, investment in development is non-negotiable.”

articles.title: What Happened to Gwadar’s Rights Movement?
articles.full_text:
Haq Do Tehreek, the movement that once brought the world’s attention to Gwadar’s longstanding grievances, is a pale shadow of its former self.
Residents of Gwadar participate in a Haq do Tehreek protest at Gwadar in Pakistan, Nov. 20, 2022,
In November 2021, thousands of people rallied and participated in sit-ins along Gwadar’s Harbor Road, demanding rights for the local Baloch people. What came to be known as the “Haq Do Tehreek” (Give Us Our Rights Movement) began mainly as a movement of the fishing community to address their grievances. But soon, women, children, men, and people from different walks of life joined the protests, making it the largest mass mobilization in the history of Gwadar.
Gwadar is not just another town or port. Located on Pakistan’s Makran coast, it sits near the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz. Its proximity to this strategic waterway through which a significant amount of the world’s oil and gas passes, and China’s investment and foothold at its port, have cemented Gwadar’s role not only in regional trade but also in global maritime geopolitics.
Gwadar port and Balochistan’s mineral wealth have, however, long been points of contention and have contributed to the turbulent political situation in the province.
As the gateway of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), Gwadar port triggered great expectations in the early days of the port’s construction. Many believed that the fishing town would be transformed into a modern city, bringing prosperity to Gwadar’s residents. But two decades later, most of the expectations are unfulfilled.
In 2021, the Haq Do Tehreek emerged. The movement drew attention to the wide gap between the development and prosperity that Gwadar port promised and the everyday realities that the majority of its residents encountered. It brought people together to demand basic services like water, electricity, economic security, a ban on illegal fishing and trawling, freedom of movement, and relief from excessive security checkpoints, along with a list of other longstanding grievances.
Thus, in 2021, the Haq Do Tehreek became a symbol of resistance, and an example of how collective action and local mass mobilization of people, mainly the fishing community, could bring their long-neglected grievances to the forefront.
One of the reasons for the Haq Do Tehreek’s rapid rise and mass participation was its leadership. Maulana Hidayat-ur-Rehman, the leader of Haq Do Tehreek, was already politically active as a member of the Jamaat-e-Islami (JI). He also belonged to the fishing community, rather than to elite or established political families. This helped him connect with the masses. Consequently, JI activists and fishing communities participated in large numbers in the movement. In December 2022, they participated in large numbers to protest and blockade the entrance to Gwadar port and the East Bay Expressway.
The Haq Do Tehreek began as a peaceful movement. However, it soon escalated and violence erupted. A police constable died from injuries in the unrest; more than 100 people were arrested and restrictions were imposed on public gatherings and telecommunications.
With the government cracking down on the movement, Rehman came under scrutiny, forcing him to go into hiding in December 2022. When he re-emerged weeks later in January 2023 and presented himself before the courts to surrender and seek bail, he was arrested. He denied allegations linking him to the constable’s death and was then granted bail by the Supreme Court in May 2023. Mass support for the Maulana increased after his arrest. In February 2024, Rehman contested provincial elections and won a seat in the Balochistan assembly.
His participation in elections was controversial; while some considered his contesting the election as a route for pursuing the movement’s demands through formal politics, others opposed it, seeing it as a step that would weaken the Haq Do Tehreek. There were doubts whether Rehman, who had built his reputation by challenging the authorities, could deliver results from within the same political system.
Many conspiracy theories circulated at that time. Some believed that Rehman’s political rise and participation in elections were engineered by the state. After all, his entry into the provincial assembly served the government’s interest, as the unrelenting rallies and mass protests that he led were putting pressure on the local police and undermining the law and order situation in an already restive province.
So, has Rehman, as a legislator in the Balochistan assembly, been successful in getting the grievances of Gwardar’s residents addressed? The results are mixed. Illegal fishing and trawling, which were major concerns during the protests, continue unabated, as do the presence of innumerable security checkpoints and shortages of water and electricity.
Although such issues cannot be resolved overnight, the people of Gwadar cannot help but wonder what the movement achieved through its leaders joining formal politics.
The Haq Do Tehreek has transformed over the last couple of years. From a grassroots movement, it has evolved into a political party. Since the 2024 provincial elections, Haq Do Tehreek is listed as a political party with Pakistan’s Election Commission. Maulana’s political party is listed as Haq Do Tehreek on the Balochistan Assembly’s website.
Haq Do Tehreek no longer conducts mass mobilizations, aside from a long march from Quetta to Islamabad in July 2025 that Rehman led to pressure the federal government to address longstanding Baloch grievances, including enforced disappearances, restrictions on border trade, and illegal trawling. Even then, some claimed the march was organized by JI, others described it as the “Haq Do Balochistan Long March.”
The movement also suffered a setback with the death of its secretary-general, Hafeez Kiazai, in a road accident in March 2026.
Rehman is reportedly taking up issues pertaining to the fisherfolk in the provincial assembly. In October 2026, he chaired a meeting of the Balochistan Assembly’s Standing Committee on Fisheries in Gwadar to review the proposed Balochistan Fisheries and Aquaculture Bill 2026. The meeting brought together fishermen and other stakeholders to discuss reforms to protect their livelihoods and marine resources.
However, Gwadar’s Haq Do Tehreek has clearly lost the momentum and energy it once displayed. The massive rallies that were seen in 2021-2023 are no longer visible.
The movement may have handed over its struggle to formal politics, but formal politics also comes with its own constraints. After all, blaming and criticizing the very system one has become a part of is a contradiction in itself.

articles.title: To Import or Build? Southeast Asia’s Rolling Stock Dilemma
articles.full_text:
Some of the region’s governments are moving toward manufacturing their own rolling stock – but this comes with trade-offs.
A train arrives at Semut station in Surabaya, Indonesia.
Urban rail systems are growing fast across Southeast Asia. This is fueling demand for rolling stock – the train cars that actually carry millions of riders around town every day. The most common option is to import trainsets from established industry leaders in China, Japan, South Korea, or Europe. But some countries in Southeast are turning to domestic firms to meet their orders. This raises an obvious question: is this wise?
The trade-offs are clear enough. Importing trains from an established global brand like China’s CRRC means you are buying a proven product, with after-sales service and support that makes it easier to maintain the trains. Sometimes foreign firms also provide electronic systems like signalling, which makes system integration easier. For many rail providers, this is a fine deal. Metro and commuter rail systems in Bangkok and Manila rely mainly on imported rolling stock.
But some countries want more. They want to manufacture the rolling stock domestically because they believe it will generate local jobs, create long-term value, and develop important skills and technical expertise. If done well, it will allow domestic firms to grow and export their products. Indonesia is a prominent example of this strategy, with state-owned INKA producing rolling stock for the local market and for export.
INKA’s main customer is the state-owned railway company, KAI, with which it is currently in the process of merging. If you have ever traveled on an intercity train in Java it most likely was made by INKA. More recently, INKA supplied the rolling stock for the Greater Jakarta LRT and has been delivering new trainsets for Jakarta’s large, aging and very busy commuter rail system, the KRL.
INKA is a classic case of industrial policy. Rather than relying on foreign firms, the government requires KAI to procure some of its rolling stock from INKA and places restrictions on imports. This guarantees INKA a minimum level of orders while also protecting it from foreign competition, providing the train-maker some breathing room to develop industrial capabilities it might not otherwise be able to.
But here’s the catch. For such industrial policy to be effective, INKA needs to deliver the goods. It must deliver rolling stock on time and that meets basic quality standards. It must show evidence that it is making progress toward mastery of more complex technologies, skills and production capabilities. The government can bend the market to give a state-owned firm a leg up, but the firm needs to prove this intervention is worth it. Industrial policy fails when firms don’t make good use of the strategic advantage they have been given.
At the moment, INKA is struggling to deliver the goods. The train cars built for the LRT in 2023 were plagued with problems, including electrical and mechanical issues. Almost as soon as they went into service, many had to be pulled out and modified. The LRT project was run mainly by Indonesian SOEs, so the fact that it experienced growing pains was not necessarily evidence of policy failure. The key was that domestic firms, including INKA, learned from these mistakes and used them to improve.
In recent weeks, rolling stock made by INKA for Jakarta’s commuter rail system has been malfunctioning, throwing commutes into chaos. Doors are getting stuck open, forcing trains out of service. Seven cars were recalled after KAI raised concerns about structural weakness in the undercarriage. KAI is seeking special permission from the government to import used rolling stock from Japan to meet immediate operational needs while these issues are worked out. Public anger and scrutiny are rising.
Similar attempts by other home-grown firms in the region also have spotty records. In 2011, Malaysia’s Scomi won a nearly 500 million ringgit contract to supply trainsets for the Kuala Lumpur monorail. The rolling stock was delivered late, and faced performance and safety issues. The procurement became embroiled in legal disputes, and Scomi was eventually dissolved. So INKA is not alone in facing hurdles as it tries to expand its footprint. But if the government is to continue aiding such efforts, INKA needs to start delivering the goods.
This is especially true now that intra-ASEAN competition is intensifying. Vietnamese conglomerate Vingroup just announced it was launching a joint venture with France’s Alstom to co-produce 200 trainsets for the Hanoi metro under a technology licensing agreement. This is a very large and ambitious project, which would represent a major step-up in capabilities for Vingroup and Vietnam’s domestic railway industry. Of course, Vingroup has a history of taking huge swings that don’t always pan out. So we will have to see.
Most urban rail systems in Southeast Asia simply import their trains, working with established manufacturers who can deliver a proven product and after-sales service and support. For some countries, domestic manufacturing is a more important goal and the state will intervene to give local firms a head-start. Ultimately, no amount of state support or industrial policy can cover up for production failings that leave commuters stranded with unreliable products. The trains must run, and local firms like INKA must deliver the goods. Otherwise, the whole logic of industrial policy comes flying off the rails.
Urban rail systems are growing fast across Southeast Asia. This is fueling demand for rolling stock – the train cars that actually carry millions of riders around town every day. The most common option is to import trainsets from established industry leaders in China, Japan, South Korea, or Europe. But some countries in Southeast are turning to domestic firms to meet their orders. This raises an obvious question: is this wise?
The trade-offs are clear enough. Importing trains from an established global brand like China’s CRRC means you are buying a proven product, with after-sales service and support that makes it easier to maintain the trains. Sometimes foreign firms also provide electronic systems like signalling, which makes system integration easier. For many rail providers, this is a fine deal. Metro and commuter rail systems in Bangkok and Manila rely mainly on imported rolling stock.
But some countries want more. They want to manufacture the rolling stock domestically because they believe it will generate local jobs, create long-term value, and develop important skills and technical expertise. If done well, it will allow domestic firms to grow and export their products. Indonesia is a prominent example of this strategy, with state-owned INKA producing rolling stock for the local market and for export.
INKA’s main customer is the state-owned railway company, KAI, with which it is currently in the process of merging. If you have ever traveled on an intercity train in Java it most likely was made by INKA. More recently, INKA supplied the rolling stock for the Greater Jakarta LRT and has been delivering new trainsets for Jakarta’s large, aging and very busy commuter rail system, the KRL.
INKA is a classic case of industrial policy. Rather than relying on foreign firms, the government requires KAI to procure some of its rolling stock from INKA and places restrictions on imports. This guarantees INKA a minimum level of orders while also protecting it from foreign competition, providing the train-maker some breathing room to develop industrial capabilities it might not otherwise be able to.
But here’s the catch. For such industrial policy to be effective, INKA needs to deliver the goods. It must deliver rolling stock on time and that meets basic quality standards. It must show evidence that it is making progress toward mastery of more complex technologies, skills and production capabilities. The government can bend the market to give a state-owned firm a leg up, but the firm needs to prove this intervention is worth it. Industrial policy fails when firms don’t make good use of the strategic advantage they have been given.
At the moment, INKA is struggling to deliver the goods. The train cars built for the LRT in 2023 were plagued with problems, including electrical and mechanical issues. Almost as soon as they went into service, many had to be pulled out and modified. The LRT project was run mainly by Indonesian SOEs, so the fact that it experienced growing pains was not necessarily evidence of policy failure. The key was that domestic firms, including INKA, learned from these mistakes and used them to improve.
In recent weeks, rolling stock made by INKA for Jakarta’s commuter rail system has been malfunctioning, throwing commutes into chaos. Doors are getting stuck open, forcing trains out of service. Seven cars were recalled after KAI raised concerns about structural weakness in the undercarriage. KAI is seeking special permission from the government to import used rolling stock from Japan to meet immediate operational needs while these issues are worked out. Public anger and scrutiny are rising.
Similar attempts by other home-grown firms in the region also have spotty records. In 2011, Malaysia’s Scomi won a nearly 500 million ringgit contract to supply trainsets for the Kuala Lumpur monorail. The rolling stock was delivered late, and faced performance and safety issues. The procurement became embroiled in legal disputes, and Scomi was eventually dissolved. So INKA is not alone in facing hurdles as it tries to expand its footprint. But if the government is to continue aiding such efforts, INKA needs to start delivering the goods.
This is especially true now that intra-ASEAN competition is intensifying. Vietnamese conglomerate Vingroup just announced it was launching a joint venture with France’s Alstom to co-produce 200 trainsets for the Hanoi metro under a technology licensing agreement. This is a very large and ambitious project, which would represent a major step-up in capabilities for Vingroup and Vietnam’s domestic railway industry. Of course, Vingroup has a history of taking huge swings that don’t always pan out. So we will have to see.
Most urban rail systems in Southeast Asia simply import their trains, working with established manufacturers who can deliver a proven product and after-sales service and support. For some countries, domestic manufacturing is a more important goal and the state will intervene to give local firms a head-start. Ultimately, no amount of state support or industrial policy can cover up for production failings that leave commuters stranded with unreliable products. The trains must run, and local firms like INKA must deliver the goods. Otherwise, the whole logic of industrial policy comes flying off the rails.

The trade-offs are clear enough. articles.title: China Coast Guard Says It Monitored Philippine Resupply Mission at Contested Shoal
articles.full_text:
Last month, Manila accused Beijing of obstructing a similar mission to resupply troops stationed aboard a grounded warship on the shoal.
A photo released by the Armed Forces of the Philippines that claims to show a China Coast Guard vessel firing a water cannon in the vicinity of Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea, Aug. 20, 2025.
The China Coast Guard (CCG) said that it monitored a Philippine delivery of “living necessities” to troops stationed at Second Thomas ​Shoal yesterday, a month after the Philippines accused the CCG of obstructing a similar mission.
Manila undertakes periodic missions to resupply the small unit of marines stationed aboard the BRP Sierra Madre, a grounded World War II-era warship that functions as the Philippines’ foothold at the contested shoal.
In a statement yesterday that was paraphrased by Xinhua, CCG spokesperson Jiang Lue said that it had “inquired and verified the Philippine vessel conducting the delivery, and monitored the entire process.” He added that the CCG “will continue to conduct law-enforcement and rights-protection operations” in the Spratly Islands and at Second Thomas Shoal, which Beijing refers to as Ren’ai Jiao.
China claims the majority of the South China Sea, including the entire Spratly archipelago, where the Philippines currently occupies nine features. In recent years, these have become the subject of a Chinese pressure campaign that has led to confrontations between the two sides, some involving the use of ramming tactics and high-pressure water cannons by the CCG.
Second Thomas Shoal has been a particular focus of Beijing’s efforts. Yesterday’s resupply mission, which has not been confirmed by Manila, came just under a month after the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) accused the CCG of obstructing a resupply ​mission to the BRP Sierra Madre. The vessel was grounded on the shoal in 1999 in order to strengthen the Philippines’ claim over it, an act that China considers illegal.
According to PCG spokesperson Jay Tarriela, the mission on September 25 was “temporarily suspended after a CCG vessel carried out dangerous maneuvers” against the Philippine resupply vessel M/V Lapu-Lapu. The maneuvers “put Filipino personnel at risk” and prevented the mission from being completed, he said. In July, a Philippine marine was injured in a melee with Chinese sailors after a CCG boat carrying eight personnel approached within close range of the BRP Sierra Madre.
These incidents broke a period of relative calm at Second Thomas Shoal, following a string of increasingly dangerous confrontations between the two sides in 2023 and 2024. After a physical clash between the two sides in July 2024 that left eight Philippine naval personnel injured, including one who lost a thumb, Beijing and Manila agreed to de-escalate the situation at Second Thomas Shoal, reaching a “provisional understanding” that allowed the Philippines to resupply the Sierra Madre without hindrance.
While the agreement appeared for a time to have calmed the situation at Second Thomas Shoal and prevented it from spiraling into a broader conflict, the two sides have disputed the details of the arrangement.
China argues that the resupply operations must be reported in advance and subjected to its inspection. In its statement yesterday, for instance, the CCG stated that the Philippines had completed its resupply missions with China’s “approval,” in line with the earlier “provisional arrangement.” The Philippines does not acknowledge any obligation to comply with such conditions or inform China of resupply missions.
The recent incidents suggest that the tacit understanding to avoid further clashes at Second Thomas Shoal has now collapsed, and the feature has once again moved to the frontline of the maritime disputes between China and the Philippines.

articles.title: The Impending Impeachment Conviction of Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte
articles.full_text:
Four months into her impeachment trial in the Senate, the political winds are starting to turn against Duterte.
The Philippine Senate holds a hearing in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Oct. 13, 2026.
Recent political realignments in the Philippines suggest that a guilty verdict has already been secured in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
The House of Representatives twice impeached Duterte, but it was only in July that a trial was convened by the Senate, which needs to deliver a verdict on the allegations that the vice president committed high crimes and betrayed public trust.
In several articles, I wrote about the slim prospect of a conviction given the dominance of Duterte supporters in the Senate. Even President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. publicly rejected a “divisive” trial, which eventually led to the archiving of the initial impeachment complaint in 2025.
The push to remove the vice president from office became clearer in the second half of the year when the Senate convened an impeachment court, and when the president allowed Duterte’s tax and bank records to be used as evidence. The prosecution panel’s first presentation was about the alleged grave threats made by Duterte against the First Family, which was intended to consolidate the ranks of the president’s supporters.
The start of the trial coincided with the filing of non-bailable plunder charges against two pro-Duterte senators, which prevented them from attending the impeachment sessions. Another pro-Duterte senator, who was a former police chief, went into hiding after an arrest warrant was issued against him by the International Criminal Court for his role in the bloody “war on drugs” during the previous administration of Rodrigo Duterte, the vice president’s father.
During the course of the trial, one member of the Senate Duterte bloc decided to join the majority. Another member went abroad to seek medical treatment, but it became an indefinite leave after a plunder complaint was filed against her. The absence of pro-Duterte senators has made it easier for the majority to lower the number of votes needed to convict the vice president. The Senate decision to lower the voting threshold was questioned by pro-Duterte lawyers at the Supreme Court, but the latter dismissed their petition on procedural grounds.
The prosecution’s presentation of evidence on the alleged unexplained wealth of Duterte and her husband provided the public with new information about the vice president’s undeclared assets and business dealings. Some of the suspicious financial transactions were traced to China, which prompted some Marcos officials to comment that it should be further investigated as a potential national security threat.
Duterte has denied ownership of the bank accounts and properties mentioned during her trial. She also insisted that doing business in China is legitimate. Nevertheless, she still needs to explain the mismatch and omissions in her statement of assets as a government official, and the large amount of earnings from her husband’s vague business operations in China.
The prosecution is confident that they can get a guilty verdict on the issue of Duterte’s unexplained wealth, and they made a bold move by dropping other charges in their presentation, including the grave threats against the First Family, misuse of confidential funds, and bribery.
This could also signal that there is now enough number of votes in the Senate to convict Duterte. The impeachment trial may last until the end of the year unless the defense panel decides to present additional witnesses to extend the sessions until early 2027.
The decision to limit the impeachment case to the issue of unexplained wealth has drawn mixed reactions. On one hand, it has been welcomed for expediting the trial and allowing the prosecution to focus on an issue with strong evidence. But it has also been criticized for its potential to undermine the public clamor for accountability, especially since the allegation about the anomalous spending of confidential funds was dropped from the charges. Critics said it could set a precedent by reducing the impeachment process to a transactional matter involving legislators and the presidential office, instead of upholding its role in exacting full accountability against erring officials.
Duterte’s political future will soon be decided by the Senate. Whatever happens, she can take comfort that she still leads in presidential election surveys. If she is convicted, her younger brother could run for president. So far, Marcos has no clear successor, which still makes the Dutertes the formidable team to beat at the 2028 presidential election.
In the meantime, the public awaits the counterarguments and evidence to be presented by Duterte’s legal team in the second half of the impeachment trial.
